title: Evolution of the ribosomal exit tunnel through the eyes of the nascent chain.
journal: Nucleic Acids Research 54(13), Jul 2026 (PMID 42411408, PMC13338714). Open access, CC-BY.
data_url: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18079792 (Zenodo, CC-BY-4.0, 3 zip files + README.md, 28.1 GB total). Code: https://github.com/dydymos/ribotunnel (notebooks and Python only, no data tables).

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Read the full Zenodo record metadata and the 2,709-byte README. Listed the complete contents of all three zip archives using HTTP range requests (11 requests, no bulk download): archaea.zip 2.50 GB/226 entries, bacteria.zip 9.10 GB/824 entries, eukaryota.zip 16.49 GB/1,489 entries. Counted file types and organism folders in each. Listed the whole GitHub repository tree.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: That the paper analysed 64 ribosome structures (20 bacteria, 38 eukaryotes, 6 archaea), the molecular dynamics protocol (3 replicas, 5x10^7 steps, GROMACS 2021, structure-based all-atom model), the 1 Angstrom voxel grid, and the reported asphericity range of 0 to 0.55 in bacteria. Supplementary Tables S1-S5 (the lists of PDB structures used) were not retrievable: the Europe PMC supplementary-files endpoint timed out after 135 seconds.

a1_downloadable.note: Fully open on Zenodo under CC-BY-4.0, no login. I confirmed by HTTP range request that all three archives serve bytes and parse as valid zip files.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: There is no table anywhere in the deposit. The 2,539 entries are only .xtc simulation trajectories (840 files), .mrc volumetric density maps (275), .gro coordinate files (245) and .pdb structures (280) - zero .csv, .tsv, .txt, .dat or .xvg files. The data availability statement promises 'calculated cross-sectional area profiles', and they are simply not there. Any prediction target (tunnel width, asphericity, accessibility) would have to be reconstructed from volumetric maps with VMD, ChimeraX and GROMACS before a single row exists.

a3_inputs_present.note: The structural input is physically present: 280 tunnel.pdb files (one per organism per nascent-chain length, 0.10-0.40 MB each) hold the actual atoms lining each exit tunnel, so no accession lookups would be needed.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are stated in the Methods (1 Angstrom voxel grid, cross-sectional area in square Angstroms, asphericity dimensionless 0-1) and the file formats are standard, but there is no tabular file in which a units column could exist.

a5_enough_rows.note: The deposit contains 56 organisms (18 bacteria, 33 eukaryotes, 5 archaea), verified by counting second-level folder names in all three archives. Even counting each organism-by-nascent-chain-length combination separately gives at most 275 units (the number of averaged occupancy maps). The checklist floor is ~1,500 labelled rows, or ~400 for classification; the only natural classification label here is domain of life, with 3 classes and 5 archaeal examples.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 28.1 GB compressed across three archives; the smallest single archive is 2.50 GB and the smallest useful subset (the 275 averaged occupancy maps at ~6 MB each) is ~1.8 GB but is only reachable by downloading whole multi-gigabyte zips.
a6_fits_laptop.note: Over the ~5 GB working-set limit and far over the project's 50 MB per-file download cap. Analysis also needs GROMACS, VMD and ChimeraX, none of which is a Python dependency, and reading the 840 trajectory files is a molecular-dynamics post-processing job, not a table load.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Direct mismatch I measured in the files. The paper states 64 structures (20 bacteria, 38 eukaryotes, 6 archaea); the archives contain 56 organism folders (18 bacteria, 33 eukaryotes, 5 archaea). The deposit was published 2025-12-29 and is linked as a supplement to the bioRxiv preprint, so it appears to predate the final 64-structure version, and I cannot tell from the files which count is right.

a8_label_provenance.note: Nothing here is a physical measurement. Every quantity (occupancy map, cross-sectional area, asphericity) is the output of a structure-based molecular dynamics simulation run on the very ribosome structure that would serve as the model input, so the label is computed from the features - leakage by construction, and a ceiling set by the simulation rather than by biology.

existing_models.name: ROSE (Ribosome Stalling Estimator), a convolutional neural network predicting ribosome stalling from messenger RNA sequence (Zhang et al., Cell Systems 2017)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported up to 18.4% improvement in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve over earlier predictors on ribosome-profiling-derived stalling sites; split details not checked.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not checked - this model addresses a different task (stalling from sequence), not exit-tunnel geometry.

existing_models.name: Riboformer, a transformer predicting context-dependent translation dynamics at codon resolution (Nature Communications 2024)
existing_models.score_and_split: Codon-level prediction of ribosome density changes across ribosome-profiling datasets; exact numbers and splits not checked.

existing_models.name: Coarse-grained nascent-chain/exit-tunnel simulation pipeline (O'Brien lab, Biophysical Journal 2025; github.com/obrien-lab/cg_simtk_protein_folding)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not a machine-learning model: an automated physics pipeline that extracts exit-tunnel geometry from any ribosome structure and builds a bead model. It is the closest competitor to this paper's approach and already solves the geometry-extraction step without learning.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Electrostatic and dynamic effects on nascent-chain escape.

backbone.name: No sensible backbone. ESM-2 (a protein language model) takes sequences, not tunnel shapes; a 3D convolutional network on the .mrc occupancy maps would have to be trained from scratch on 275 maps.
backbone.hardware: Not applicable - the blocker is 56 examples, not compute.
backbone.licence: Data CC-BY-4.0, code permissive; licensing is not the problem.

integration.partner_dataset: The Protein Data Bank (~2,830 ribosome entries, per this paper's own search) and the Ribosome Analysis Database (RADtool) are joinable on PDB identifier, and UniProt/NCBI taxonomy identifiers would link organisms.
integration.join_key: PDB ID (the 4-letter organism folder names are organism abbreviations, not PDB codes, so the mapping lives only in the unretrievable Supplementary Tables S1-S3)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does exit-tunnel shape predict which proteins a given organism can fold co-translationally? - but answering it needs per-protein folding measurements that this deposit does not contain and that exist for only a handful of proteins.

controls.positive_control: The two textbook constriction sites formed by proteins uL4 and uL22 should appear as narrow points in any correctly computed tunnel profile - a good sanity check on a pipeline, but it is a reproduction of the paper's figure, not a model test.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling across the 3 domains of life is runnable but meaningless at 5 archaeal examples.
controls.external_validation: None available. There is no second independent dataset of nascent-chain occupancy maps, and no publication-year or source column to split on.

honest_claim_h3: Any model built here could only claim: 'from a ribosome structure, we reproduce the tunnel shape that a structure-based molecular dynamics simulation of that same structure would have produced', for 56 organisms chosen as one representative per species from the Protein Data Bank.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a ribosome's three-dimensional structure to predict the shape of the tunnel its newborn protein chain must squeeze through.
plain_idea.train_on: The atoms lining the protein exit tunnel of each ribosome, supplied as 280 structure files covering 56 organisms at five nascent-chain lengths (10, 20, 30, 40 and 60 amino acids). I verified these counts by listing the archives.
plain_idea.predict: The tunnel's functional shape along its axis - cross-sectional area in square Angstroms and asphericity (how far from circular, 0 to 1). The true answer comes not from any experiment but from this paper's own molecular dynamics simulations, three replicas of 50 million steps each, which is exactly why the project fails.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: If it worked, structural biologists studying antibiotic binding or co-translational folding could screen tunnel shape across thousands of ribosome structures without running simulations. As posed it cannot work: there are 56 examples and the answer is derived from the input.

ml_idea: The project considered was: predict functional exit-tunnel geometry (cross-sectional area and asphericity profiles) from ribosome structure, so that tunnel shape could be screened across the ~2,830 ribosome entries in the Protein Data Bank without running molecular dynamics - effectively learning a fast surrogate for this paper's simulation pipeline. It dies on three counts: 56 organisms, no tabular label of any kind, and a label that is the simulation output of the input structure.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, nothing timed. Peak RAM is low because the 275 occupancy maps are ~6 MB each and stream easily; the cost is the 28.1 GB download and 40-plus hours of molecular-dynamics post-processing with VMD, ChimeraX and GROMACS to turn volumetric maps into numbers, work that has to happen before any row exists.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the organism folders inside the archives. I did this with 11 HTTP range requests and no bulk download: 56 folders, versus 64 structures claimed in the paper, and zero tabular files. That single count kills the project in under five minutes.

verdict_reason: Fails five Part A killers, all verified in the files. A2: the deposit holds only simulation trajectories and volumetric density maps - no table, and the cross-sectional area profiles the data availability statement promises are absent. A5: 56 organisms (275 organism-by-length units), against a floor of ~1,500. A6: 28.1 GB, with the smallest archive at 2.50 GB and analysis requiring GROMACS, VMD and ChimeraX. A7: 56 organism folders versus the paper's stated 64 structures, and the files cannot say which is right. A8: every candidate label is computed by molecular dynamics from the same structure that would be the input, so it is leakage by construction. The paper is a genuinely nice piece of comparative structural biology; it just is not a machine-learning dataset.
